en.title: Breakfast
en.summary: What people eat and drink in the morning, and how to order or offer a meal.

paragraphs: Sophie and her husband are having breakfast on a Saturday.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: What would you like for breakfast?

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: Two eggs and some toast, please. Is there any marmalade?

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: Yes, it is in the cupboard. Would you like tea or coffee?

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.text: Tea, please, with a little milk.

lines.speaker: Sophie
lines.text: I will make a pot. Do you want some orange juice too?

paragraphs: **1. Some and any with food.** Use some in positive sentences and offers, and any in questions and negatives. Food words like milk and toast are uncountable. See Introduction to Grammar: Articles and determiners.

blocks.html:
TypeExample
positiveThere is some toast.
questionIs there any marmalade?
negativeThere isn't any milk.
offerWould you like some tea?

paragraphs: **2. Would like is polite.** It states a wish without sounding rude. Use I would like... to order and Would you like...? to offer. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

blocks.html:
FunctionExample
orderI would like two eggs, please.
offerWould you like some coffee?
acceptYes, please.
refuseNo, thank you.

items: A **full English breakfast** has eggs, bacon, sausages, beans, tomatoes and toast.
**Marmalade** is made from oranges; **jam** is made from other fruit.

paragraphs: In the United States a typical breakfast includes pancakes, eggs or cereal with coffee. Many working people have just a coffee and something quick.
